title: Uninformed Search: BFS, DFS & UCS
html:
Uninformed (blind) strategies know nothing about where the goal is — only how to generate successors and test for the goal. They differ solely in which frontier node to expand next.

StrategyFrontierExpandsFinds
Breadth-first (BFS)FIFO queueShallowest node first — level by levelThe path with the fewest steps
Depth-first (DFS)LIFO stack (or recursion)Deepest node firstSome path — often long
Uniform-cost (UCS)Priority queue on path cost g(n)Cheapest-so-far node firstThe lowest-cost path (Dijkstra's algorithm)

BFS and DFS on the Romania map

The classic textbook example: drive from Arad to Bucharest. Roads have lengths in km; the neighbour order below is the order roads were listed.

BFS finds the route with the fewest roads (3), but it is not the shortest in km. DFS dives down whichever branch it pushed last and returns a much longer route.

Uniform-cost search

UCS always expands the frontier node with the lowest path cost g(n). It must test for the goal when a node is popped, not when it is generated — a cheaper route to the goal may still be on the frontier.

Key point

UCS is Dijkstra's algorithm stopped at the goal. It expands nodes in rings of increasing cost — in all directions, because it has no idea where Bucharest is. Adding that knowledge gives A* (see Informed Search).

BFSDFSUCS
Complete?Yes (finite b)No in infinite spaces or with loops (tree search); yes for finite graph searchYes if every step cost ≥ ε > 0
Optimal?Only if all step costs are equalNoYes
TimeO(bᵈ)O(bᵐ)O(b^(1 + ⌊C*/ε⌋))
SpaceO(bᵈ) — keeps the whole frontierO(bm) — only the current path + siblingsO(b^(1 + ⌊C*/ε⌋))
Watch out

BFS's real problem is memory, not time: at b = 10, depth 10 means ~10¹⁰ nodes in memory — terabytes. DFS uses linear memory but can wander down an infinite branch.

When is BFS optimal?

When every action has the same cost (or cost is a non-decreasing function of depth). Then the shallowest goal is also the cheapest. With varied step costs use UCS.

Why must UCS test the goal on expansion rather than generation?

When the goal is first generated it may be via an expensive edge (Fagaras → Bucharest, total 450) while a cheaper route (via Pitesti, 418) is still on the frontier. Waiting until the goal is popped guarantees it's the cheapest.

Is Dijkstra's algorithm the same as UCS?

Essentially yes. Dijkstra computes shortest paths from a source to all nodes in an explicit graph; UCS stops at the goal and works on implicit graphs generated on the fly.
